chunks.content: In the United States, ~​​​​​​60% of patients diagnosed with breast cancer undergo breast-conserving surgery (BCS) for nonpalpable tumors, necessitating tumor localization. – Wire localization (WL), where a thin metal wire is placed into the tumor immediately before surgery, has been the most common approach for the localization of nonpalpable breast tumors, even though there are several disadvantages to the technique. WL relies on the immediate availability of a radiologist and radiology suite, ideally located within the surgery facility, so that patient transport does not compromise wire placement. WL can also be uncomfortable for the patient since multiple wires may protrude from the breast. Therefore, WL has to be performed as close to the surgery as possible to avoid wire migration as well as minimize patient discomfort. In addition, the surgeon must understand the 3-dimensional wire location for optimal incision placement. Localization of specific lymph nodes in the axilla is difficult with a wire due to the anatomic location. Due in part to these challenges, other technologies have been developed, including intraoperative ultrasound, radioactive intraoperative occult lesion localization, hematoma localization, radar localization, magnetic seed localization such as Magseed, SAVI Scout, and radioactive seed localization (RSL). RSL entails inserting a single standard I-125 titanium seed into a nonpalpable breast lesion using mammographic or sonographic guidance. The patient is exposed to minimal radiation, similar to a 2-view mammogram, ~2 cGy. , A gamma probe is then used to guide excision. Due to its long half-life (59 d), the seed can be placed several days before surgery, improving scheduling flexibility and dissociating the surgeon from the radiologist. Also, the seed is embedded in the breast tissue, like the marking clip, and therefore causes less patient discomfort. Known drawbacks of RSL include seed migration, inability to reposition, and bracketing difficulty. Concerns regarding radioactive contamination have been addressed by traps that buffer the seed from vacuum suction systems. Most studies comparing RSL and WL have been retrospective or nonrandomized in nature. In the United States, only 2 small, single-center, randomized controlled trials have been conducted, which demonstrated comparable rates of positive margins, re-excision rates, and excised tissue volumes for RSL and WL. , Three other randomized controlled trials conducted outside the United States used surgical volume, specimen margins, surgical duration, and need for reoperation to compare the 2 methods. – RSL was deemed an acceptable alternative to WL in all 5 of these randomized controlled trials, particularly due to similar negative margin and re-excision rates. In 2 of the trials, RSL also demonstrated better satisfaction scores, with patients reporting less pain and better convenience and surgeons reporting less difficulty. , As the patient journey during their breast cancer diagnosis and treatment is often distressing, it is important to focus on aspects of care such as patient satisfaction. With health care costs increasing in the United States, especially in cancer care, localization procedure costs should be considered. Four studies have looked at cost, but only one was conducted in the United States. There are mixed data on the cost efficiency between RSL and WL. – However, some data suggest that overall complication and re-excision rates are lower with RSL, which may decrease total cost. Our study is the largest randomized, controlled trial in the United States comparing RSL and WL in patients with breast cancer. The aim of this randomized controlled trial was to compare RSL and WL in patients with nonpalpable, unifocal breast cancer. We focused not only on surgical margins but also on time efficiency, health care costs, complication rates, and patient, surgeon, pathologist, and radiologist satisfaction. METHODS Study Design This study was a single-center, unblinded, randomized, prospective clinical trial conducted between July 2015 and January 2021. The primary objective was to compare negative margin rates following initial resection between patients randomized to RSL or WL for the treatment of breast cancer. Secondary objectives included time from consultation to operation, time in radiology, surgery, and pathology, tissue weight, satisfaction, cost, adverse events, and complications. The institutional review board approved this consent-based study. Enrollment pauses occurred in August 2015 for 5.8 months due to a personnel shortage and in March 2020 for 4.5 months due to COVID-19. Participants were recruited from and received care at 4 hospitals. Eligibility Criteria Female patients aged 29 to 99 years with a biopsy-proven malignant unifocal breast lesion requiring image-guided localization for excision by BCS were eligible. Patients with multifocal, multicentric, locally advanced disease, prior ipsilateral breast cancer, treated with neoadjuvant therapy, and currently pregnant were excluded. Eligible patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive RSL or WL in an unblinded fashion and were stratified by the surgeon and invasive status at clinical staging to reflect differing definitions of negative margins between invasive cancer and ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and potential differences between surgeons. The randomization schedule was provided by an independent statistician who was not directly involved in the study before the study opening. Before activation, the randomization schedule was made available directly in the enterprise clinical trial management system. Study participation was discussed during the initial surgical consult. Consent was obtained by the clinical trials team subsequent to this visit. Localization Procedures Wire placement was performed by 17 trained radiologists. For seed placement, one designated radiologist trained in I-125 seed technology trained all other radiologists. Two supervised cases by the designated radiologist were required before independent placement. Surgical Procedure Seven breast surgeons participated in the trial. The surgical technique was similar to the 2 localization techniques. A designated surgeon trained in I-125 seed technology trained all other surgeons. Three supervised cases by the designated surgeon were required before independent surgical use. At our institution, surgical margins are assessed by intraoperative radiography. The specimen radiograph is examined by the surgeon and radiologist to evaluate any margins of concern. Any close margins are taken as an additional margin at the time of the initial operation. End Points The primary end point was negative margin status after initial surgical resection, defined as no ink on the tumor for invasive disease and ≥2 mm from the inked margin for DCIS on pathology. – A close margin (DCIS and papillary carcinoma) was defined as <2 mm from ink on pathology. Secondary end points concerning intervals of time were defined as follows: time from initial consult to operating room for initial surgery (days), time in radiology from start to end of the localization procedure (minutes), operating room time from first incision to closure (minutes) (for patients undergoing sentinel lymph node (SLN) biopsy, the sum of time for lumpectomy and SLN biopsy), and pathology time as start to end time of specimen dissection (WL, clip identification; RSL, seed removal and clip identification). Patient, radiologist, surgeon, and pathologist/pathology assistant satisfaction was captured using a 5-point Likert-type scale, ranging from extremely negative (mapped to a numerical score of 1) to extremely positive (mapped to a numerical score of 5). Radiologists, surgeons, and pathologists/pathology assistants each completed 1 paper survey within 5 days of the procedure rating aspects of the case (procedure ease, satisfaction, and convenience). Patients completed 2 paper surveys, the first after the localization procedure (assessing pain, anxiety, ease of scheduling, and satisfaction) and the second at their postoperative visit (assessing pain, anxiety, cosmetic outcome, and satisfaction). Some dissections were performed by a pathology assistant, and some by pathologists. Adverse events were graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.0; reportable adverse events (grades 1–5) deemed related to the localization and/or surgery that required treatment or intervention were documented, alongside reported complications from the treating clinicians. Adverse event data collection concluded 30 (±5) days after the final surgery. Total charge amounts were collected for each patient’s localization and, if applicable, adverse events requiring treatment. Statistical Analysis As informed by Jakub et al, an 80% negative margin rate was expected in the WL arm. Based on a 2-sided alpha=0.05 level test, 200 randomized subjects per arm (400 total) would provide at least 80% power to declare superiority for the RSL arm, assuming the true negative margin rate in the RSL arm was 90%. All efficacy analyses included all randomized patients and were informed by the intent-to-treat principle—participants were analyzed according to the localization group they were originally assigned, regardless of the localization procedure received. All randomized patients were included in analyses of complications and adverse events, and participants were analyzed according to the localization procedure received. Negative margin rates were calculated, and the corresponding 95% CI was estimated using the Clopper–Pearson method for binomial CIs. Rates were compared between the arms based on a logistic regression model, incorporating the surface area of the excised specimen, the stratification variables of the surgeon, and presence of invasive disease component as covariates. The surgical specimen surface area was calculated as the product of skin-to-deep, medial-to-lateral, and cranial-to-caudal measurements. Time intervals, tissue weights, and surface areas were analyzed quantitatively using analysis of variance techniques. Cost Analysis An institution’s total costs are proprietary and reimbursement is dependent on insurance stakeholder; thus, standard health economics reporting methods were used to “transform cost” by applying year-specific and institution-specific cost-to-charge ratios to the total charge amount. Costs were reported from the perspective of the hospital system and inflated from year of service to 2020 US dollars using the Medical Component of Consumer Price Index. Cost analyses utilized a decision analytic model of estimated transformed costs associated with RSL or WL. The model was stratified by type of localization, SLN biopsy, subsequent re-excision, and adverse events. Exclusions included patients who had additional procedures unrelated to localization, missing billing data, a mastectomy after BCS, off study before subsequent re-excision, and surgery performed in 2021. Hypothetical scenario analysis was used to test the robustness of the cost data, which included assumed equal proportions regardless of having an SLN biopsy, subsequent re-excision, or an adverse event. RESULTS Patient Characteristics Overall, 400 patients were randomized to receive RSL (N=200) or WL (N=200) for malignant breast disease (Fig. ). Most women identified as White [333 of 400 (83%)] and non-Hispanic/Latino [376 of 400 (94%)], with a median age of 62 years [interquartile range (IQR), 54–68 y)] (Table ). Seventy-eight percent of patients (312 of 400) had cT1 disease, 85% (338 of 400) had an invasive disease component at presentation, 89% (356 of 400) were estrogen receptor positive, and 75% (300 of 400) were HER2 nonamplified. Imbalances in patient or disease characteristics between the arms were not detected. Eleven patients were taken off study before localization due to being found ineligible per protocol after screening (N=6), being withdrawn per investigator discretion (N=2), or withdrawing consent (N=3) (Fig. ). The remaining 389 patients (97%) underwent localization before BCS and completed protocol-defined procedures. One hundred percent of patients (200 of 200) randomized to WL received the WL intervention. Ninety-four percent of patients (188 of 200) randomized to RSL received the RSL intervention. Pathologists completed surveys for 379 of 389 (97%) cases; surveys were inadvertently missed in 3 RSL cases and 7 WL cases. There was no significant difference in pathologist-reported ease for RSL as compared with WL ( P =0.23) (Fig. ). Cost Results For base case analysis, which incorporated adverse events, the estimated cost of RSL was $18,500, whereas the estimated cost for WL was $17,900, a $600 difference in cost with RSL incurring a higher cost (Table ). This difference decreased to $400 when adjusted for equal probability of sentinel lymph node biopsy, re-excision, and adverse events. DISCUSSION While several randomized controlled trials in the United States have compared breast preoperative localization, , , , our study is the largest conducted to date within a high-volume center that focused on the most commonly used technologies, the wire and radioactive seed. Our study also focused on patient and physician satisfaction as well as overall cost, which has not been evaluated previously. We determined that RSL is an acceptable alternative to WL for obtaining similar negative margins. There was no difference in operating room time between the localization techniques when limiting surgery time to lumpectomy alone, and no difference in surface area of excised specimens. Furthermore, there was no significant difference in the number of adverse effects or complications. Our results are similar to those by Lovrics et al and Langhans and colleagues, which demonstrated that RSL has similar rates of positive margins, re-excision rates, and volume of tissue excised as compared with WL. , Importantly, both patient and surgeon satisfaction were higher with RSL. There was no difference in pathologist or radiologist satisfaction by localization technique; however, radiologists noted that RSL was more convenient. This was likely due, in part, because patients reported decreased pain and anxiety with the RSL procedure. A procedure is likely more convenient to a radiologist when the scheduling is more flexible, and the patient is more comfortable. Prioritizing the patient experience and exploring avenues for improvement are important during this very distressing time in a patient’s life. We found a $600 cost difference between localization techniques, with the seed being more expensive. The extra cost for RSL was due to slight increases in localization, surgery, and dissection times. The higher cost for RSL would likely be acceptable given that it is associated with decreased pain and anxiety for the patient, high surgeon satisfaction scores, and may improve operating room utilization. The cost difference decreased to $400 when switching from the base case to an equal probability scenario of sentinel lymph node biopsy, re-excision, and adverse events. Two studies conducted in Canada and the Netherlands found that RSL was more expensive than WL (98 CAD and €217, respectively), , while another study at an institution that utilized a bundled payment system found that total health care costs were on average $115 lower with RSL compared with WL. Given that costs are proprietary, it is difficult to report on specific cost findings. Therefore, our cost analyses served as estimates to determine whether a large cost difference might deter the use of either technology, which was not found to be true. Given a clear preference for the RSL technology by patients and providers, we should continue to advocate for affordable new localization technologies. Furthermore, there may be other unseen cost savings, such as decoupling the seed localization procedure from the date of operation, which may ease scheduling and improve utilization of the operating room. Limitations of this study included the pauses in enrollment. We anticipated differences in several end points during and after the learning curve period, as RSL was a new technology. However, rapid accrual resulted in a short learning curve period with few RSL cases per surgeon. Both of these factors may have contributed to the lack of differences in the end points during the study periods. A longer follow-up time may be required to demonstrate a difference in specimen weights and possibly margin rates. Another limitation is the inability to compare procedure difficulty based on patient factors such as breast size and density. We intentionally did not include body mass index as a surrogate for breast size as it is not always accurate across all body types. Breast density can affect the difficulty of a procedure, but this is dependent on the surgeon's experience and therefore is difficult to standardize. Tumor location also plays a role in procedural ease; however, additional factors such as patient breast size and density would also need to be included to fully evaluate procedural ease. Therefore, tumor location/distance from the skin or muscle was not included as a factor as it was not relevant as a singular component. In addition, there are limitations to surveys and the potential for bias based on provider preference. We limited recall bias by administering surveys after each localization procedure, surgery, and pathology sectioning. For patient surveys, it is difficult to comment on patient anxiety after the procedure as there is no baseline comparison. However, the survey questions were directed specifically to the procedure. This was a randomized controlled trial and therefore based on intent-to-treat principles, one would assume that similar factors of procedure difficulty were seen in both arms. We also intentionally did not look at other favorable factors of seed localization, such as the ability to place it 5 days before surgery, therefore optimizing surgeon time and operating room utilization. While these factors were clear RSL advantages, this did not impact our primary end point and was factored into the secondary end points in patient and surgeon satisfaction surveys. This large prospective randomized controlled trial evaluated RSL versus WL localization techniques plus included cost analysis and expanded patient-reported and physician-reported outcomes. RSL continues to be an acceptable alternative to the WL technique but more favorable in patient-reported and surgeon-reported outcomes with a wider reach in applications to breast surgery. Cost does not appear to be a deterrent to RSL use. This study is novel as it is the largest comparison of WL and RSL for nonpalpable breast tumors performed to date within the United States. Our study confirms that the RSL technology should continue to be a favorable option for the localization of breast tumors since it provides a more positive patient experience.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States and worldwide, with a 5-y survival rate of 12% ( ). PDAC is characterized by many features that pose significant challenges to its clinical management, including its indolent progression in seemingly early-stage disease and predilection for early metastasis. Additionally, in an era where immunotherapy has been employed with increasing success, PDAC has remained particularly recalcitrant to immune strategies ( ). A significant advancement in the understanding of PDAC has been the recognition of the tumor microenvironment (TME) as an important feature that makes PDAC particularly resistant to therapeutic intervention ( ). The PDAC TME consists of a complex collection of cells (e.g., tumor cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, immune cells, and neurons) woven into a dense stromal environment that, in aggregate, shields tumor cells from extraneous insults, limits immune recognition, and promotes oncogenic progression. Dissecting the molecular and cellular mechanisms that allow PDAC to orchestrate an immunosuppressive TME will be critical to devising new therapeutics and improve clinical outcomes. Among PDACs, the adenosquamous carcinoma (ASC) subtype is highly aggressive and confers a particularly poor prognosis. ASC is associated with loss-of-function mutations in several tumor suppressor genes, including TP53 , KDM6A , KMT2C , and KMT2D ( , ). The squamous epithelial characteristics of the tumor are associated with the expression of the TP63 transcription factor ( ). ASC has also been associated with mutations in the RNA helicase upstream frameshift 1 (UPF1), an integral component of the complex that mediates nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of aberrant mRNA transcripts ( ). This study reported mutations in 18 of 23 cases. Interestingly, the majority of these were intronic, clustered in intron 10, and resulting in diminished expression of the WT gene product, suggesting that it is low UPF1 expression rather than mutant protein that drives the phenotype. However, the significance of UPF1 mutations in ASC has remained controversial because another group found that a significant portion of these lesions were inherited variants rather than somatic mutations acting as functional drivers of oncogenesis ( ). Although its role as a driver of ASC is uncertain, the role of UPF1 in PDAC more broadly remains unexplored. Appreciation of UPF1 mRNA regulation has grown to include an expanding variety of processes including NMD ( ), staufen-mediated decay ( ), and structure-mediated decay ( ). Dysregulation of these pathways has been identified in many cancers, frequently through direct modulation of UPF1 expression and function. UPF1 loss can be associated with either enhanced or diminished tumor growth, depending on the context. Loss of UPF1 through a variety of mechanisms is seen in gastric cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, lung adenocarcinoma, ovarian cancer, and gliomas and is associated with increased cellular proliferation, invasion, and migration, suggesting UPF1 functions as a tumor suppressor in these cancers ( – ). On the other hand, loss of UPF1 in microsatellite unstable colorectal cancer (CRC) inhibits cellular proliferation, whereas microsatellite stable CRC is unaffected by UPF1 deficiency ( ). In this study, we interrogate the role of Upf1 in PDAC by employing an orthotopic murine model. Depletion of Upf1 led to enhanced tumor growth but only in immunocompetent animals. Mechanistic studies revealed that Upf1 loss leads to alterations in the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) resulting in the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in PDAC tumor cells, which in turn signal for the release of proinflammatory cytokines that recruit immunosuppressive myeloid cells and allow oncogenic progression. Thus, we have found that Upf1 plays an important role in mitochondrial biology in tumor cells and this cell-autonomous alteration in turn exerts a non-cell-autonomous influence on the immune TME. Results Upf1 knockout in vivo is embryonic lethal ( ) and most of the mutations associated with pancreatic ASC are noncoding but result in decreased expression of the helicase. Therefore, to model the human condition, we sought means to diminish but not eliminate Upf1 expression. To accomplish this in a genetic fashion, we developed genetically modified mice that conditionally express in the pancreas mir30Upf1, a microRNA that efficiently silences Upf1 . We generated mice transgenic for a Tet-inducible mir30Upf1, a reverse Tet activator under the control of a lox -stop- lox (LSL) cassette and Pdx-1-Cre such that mir30Upf1 would be expressed in the pancreas of mice fed tetracycline. We intended to cross these mice with the LSL -Kras 12D model of pancreatic adenocarcinoma. This precluded the use of the autochthonous model to assess the role of Upf1 suppression in PDAC. Therefore, to evaluate the influence of Upf1 suppression on pancreatic tumorigenesis, we employed RNAi to knockdown (KD) Upf1 in a mouse pancreatic cancer cell line derived from a tumor of an LSL-Kras +/G12D LSL-Tp53 R172H/+ PDX1-Cre (KPC) mouse ( ). Orthotopic implantation of Upf1 KD KPC cells into the pancreatic tail of C57BL6/J mice generated larger tumors after 21 d of growth compared to those derived from control cells ( ). We did not observe squamous metaplasia in the histological analysis of control or Upf1 deficient tumors ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 B ). We measured the relative rates of growth Upf1 KD KPC and control cells in 2D culture and found no difference ( ). Thus, the increase in tumor size cannot be explained by the accelerated growth of Upf1-deficient cells. Differences observed between in vivo and in vitro growth of tumor cells can result from the influence of the TME, including the immune system. Indeed, a complex TME has been well documented to contribute to carcinogenesis and tumor progression in PDAC. One characteristic of the PDAC TME is an immunosuppressive infiltrate that plays a significant role in shielding cancer cells from surveillance by the adaptive immune system and thereby facilitates tumor growth ( ). To test whether Upf1 expression in tumor cells affects the immune TME, we performed flow cytometric profiling of the immune infiltrate isolated from control and Upf1 KD orthotopic tumors ( ). Upf1 KD tumors had a significantly increased number of granulocyte-like myeloid-derived suppressor cells (G-MDSC; CD45 + CD11b + Ly-6G high Ly-6C + ) ( ) and a decreased number of CD8+ T cells ( ), consistent with immunosuppression. To determine the importance of the adaptive immune system in driving the differential tumor growth, we performed orthotopic implantation of control or Upf1 KD cells into NU/J animals that lack an adaptive immune system and observed no differences in tumor sizes between control and Upf1 KD cells ( ), confirming the central role of the immune system in differential growth. To determine whether these observations were reflected in human disease, we analyzed 13 treatment-naive human PDAC samples from a publicly available single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) analysis that we previously published ( ). The average expression of UPF1 in tumor cells correlated inversely with the fraction of each sample’s myeloid compartment that consisted of MDSCs ( ), consistent with our finding in mice. These results suggest that UPF1 expression in tumor cells alters the immune microenvironment. One mechanism by which tumor cells modulate the immune microenvironment is by the production of soluble factors such as cytokines that are able to both recruit immune cells and reprogram their behavior. We measured the amounts of immunomodulatory cytokines and chemokines in the cell culture supernatants of control and Upf1 KD KPC cells via Luminex Multiplex assays and found that Upf1 KD cells secrete elevated amounts of multiple proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines ( Dataset S1 ). Discussion The association of UPF1 mutations with an aggressive form of PDAC ( ) drew our attention to this RNA helicase. We found that silencing Upf1 in murine KRAS and p53 mutant PDAC cells used to generate an orthotopic tumors resulted in markedly enlarged tumors. However, we found no evidence of squamous metaplasia suggesting that Upf1 deficiency in this mouse model is not sufficient to recapitulate human ASC. The increase in tumor size required an intact adaptive immune system. This was somewhat surprising because silencing Upf1 is predicted to inhibit NMD and thereby stabilize aberrant transcripts generating neoantigens and enhancing antitumor immunity ( ). Potential for neoantigen generation notwithstanding, the result could be explained by our observation of an increase in immunosuppressive myeloid cells in Upf1 -deficient tumors. Infiltration of G-MDSCs into tumors is generally driven by proinflammatory cytokines ( ) and indeed we found that silencing Upf1 in KPC cells increased secretion of a number of such mediators, including G-CSF and CXCL2 that are known to attract G-MDSCs ( ). This raised the question of how the Upf1 RNA helicase might suppress the expression of G-CSF and CXCL2 in tumor cells. One parsimonious explanation would be through the action of regnase-1, an RNase that cooperates with Upf1 to keep inflammatory cytokine production in check by degrading their mRNAs ( ). However, we ruled out this mechanism by showing that while G-CSF mRNA stability was enhanced by silencing regnase-1, silencing Upf1 had no effect. We therefore explored other mechanisms by taking the unbiased approach of comparative transcriptomics. We found that among the pathways most perturbed in Upf1 -deficient cells was mitochondrial electron transport. We found that among the pathways most perturbed in Upf1 -deficient cells was mitochondrial electron transport. Because the mitochondrial ETC is responsible for generating cellular ROS, which is known to induce the secretion of inflammatory cytokines, we explored the relationship between Upf1 and the ETC. An effective mitochondrial electron transfer via the ETC culminating in ADP phosphorylation to generate ATP via OXPHOS is among the most tightly regulated processes within mitochondria ( ). The OXPHOS system can be modulated at different levels, including posttranslational modifications ( ) and protein complex assembly ( ), which are crucial to ensure the efficiency of the system. Pathway analysis on RNA-seq data revealed a decrease in mitochondrial transcripts after loss of Upf1 . While we validated the decrease at the protein level of a number of OXPHOS subunits, Seahorse analysis failed to show significant mitochondrial respiratory defects and the enzymatic activity of the individual ETC complexes revealed an increase in complex I activity. We also observed increased complex I protein phosphorylation and complex assembly, consistent with the enhanced activity. We can speculate that the upregulation of complex I formation and activity is a compensatory mechanism in response to the decrease in other OXPHOS subunits, explaining the observed maintenance of mitochondrial respiration. Complex I is a substantial source of ROS production by mitochondria ( ) and the likely site of ROS production in Upf1 -deficient cells. Our data support a mechanism for enhanced complex I activity that involves both the phosphorylation and content and assembly of complex I ( , , ). Interestingly, both the loss of complex I and increased activity of the complex can generate ROS. Pathological complex I deficiency leads to a very large boost in ROS production, which results in cell death ( ). In contrast, there is always some electron leak from complex I that generates low levels of ROS that increase as complex I activity increases ( ). Our data suggest that the loss of Upf1 leads to modest ROS production consistent with the electron leak caused by the activity of the complex. Rather than inducing cell death, this low-level ROS production can signal to survival pathways as part of a process known as mitohormesis, an important phenomenon in normal physiology and a critical modulator of various disease processes ( ). We found an increase in mtROS production that can be rescued by the reintroduction of Upf1 and quenched by the addition of the mitochondrial-targeted antioxidant MitoTEMPO. mtROS signaling can stimulate the production of proinflammatory cytokines ( – ). Indeed, we observed that mtROS quenching decreased G-CSF production in Upf1 -deficient cells. Interestingly, mtROS levels in control KPC cells could not be lowered by MitoTEMPO treatment, suggesting low basal levels of mtROS in these cells. Therefore, we consider that any increase in mtROS within these cells should be sufficient to stimulate signaling pathways that lead to the production of soluble factors such as immunomodulatory cytokines and chemokines that suppress the adaptive immune response to the tumor allowing tumor growth. How UPF1, an RNA helicase, regulates mitochondrial ETC activity remains to be determined. Interestingly, yeast UPF1 was originally isolated as a multicopy suppressor of mitochondrial splicing deficiency, and its deletion leads to an impairment in respiratory-dependent growth ( ). The same authors later demonstrated that overexpression of Upf1p compensates for mitochondrial splicing deficiency independently from its function in NMD in yeasts ( ). Thus, UPF1 may have a role in processing transcripts encoding ETC components. Mitochondria, ROS, and complex I are considered attractive therapeutic targets in cancer ( – ). Although antioxidants are a logical therapeutic approach, paradoxically they have been shown to accelerate the progression of lung cancer in mice ( ). Nevertheless, OXPHOS rates are highly heterogeneous among PDAC tumors, and high OXPHOS PDAC tumors are enriched in mitochondrial respiratory complex I, suggesting that PDAC patients with high complex I activity might benefit from therapies that include inhibiting this complex ( ). Introduction Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), a progressive fibrotic lung disease characterized by the histological appearance of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) and worsening respiratory symptoms, has high mortality and few treatment options , . Although the exact pathophysiological mechanisms underlying IPF remain unknown, a complex interplay of diverse cell types is involved. Sustained or repetitive lung epithelial injury is regarded as the key causative event for the disease. The injured epithelium produces profibrotic factors that contribute to subsequent fibroblast activation and myofibroblast differentiation. A persistent myofibroblast phenotype leads to excessive deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) – . Thus, dysregulated epithelial cells triggering activation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts via multiple mechanisms are central to IPF progression. Human epididymis protein 4 (HE4), encoded by the WAP four disulfide core domain protein 2 (WFDC2) gene, was originally identified in the epithelium of the distal epididymis; it was also expressed in the normal glandular epithelium of the female generative tract and breast, in respiratory epithelium, and in epithelial ovarian cancer , . Thus far, little is known regarding the biological role of HE4, although previous studies revealed that HE4 is involved in fibrotic diseases, such as kidney fibrosis and cardiac interstitial fibrosis , . Additionally, considering that HE4 is a secreted glycoprotein, multiple studies have shown that it can serve as a novel biomarker of severity in multiple types of interstitial lung disease (ILD), including rheumatoid arthritis-associated ILD, systemic sclerosis-related ILD, idiopathic inflammatory myopathy-related ILD, and IPF – . These observations illustrate the relationship between HE4 expression levels and pulmonary fibrosis (PF). However, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. It is unknown whether HE4 acts alone, or by interacting with a receptor on the cell membrane, to affect the biological behavior of critical cells in IPF. Here, we explored whether HE4 expression is associated with the clinical features of IPF severity and whether increased numbers of HE4 + epithelial cells in lung tissues are a robust feature of PF. We then interrogated the role of HE4 in various cell types in the context of PF. We found that HE4 mediated phenotypic changes in lung epithelial cells and fibroblasts, two key target cells for PF, leading to abnormal epithelial-fibroblast interaction. Moreover, we found that annexin II (ANXA2), a specific binding partner of HE4, was expressed in lung epithelial cells and fibroblasts; the interaction between HE4 and ANXA2 promoted the aberrant crosstalk described above. Finally, we developed a therapeutic strategy to inhibit HE4 activity in lung epithelium through HE4 shRNA-loaded lentivirus, offering a potential therapeutic approach for patients with IPF. HE4 is a profibrotic cytokine in the lung To experimentally determine whether HE4 has a pro- or antifibrotic role in the lung, we examined the response to BLM-induced PF in HE4 knockdown mice. We designed three lentiviral shRNA constructs for HE4 silencing and selected shRNA3 for in vivo experiments because of its silencing efficiency. Additionally, we found that lentiviruses were predominantly located in epithelial cells and BLM-induced increase of HE4 protein expression was dramatically reduced in mice administrated with HE4 shRNA (Supplementary Figs. – ). HE4 knockdown mice were significantly less susceptible to BLM and showed an increase in body weight compared with wild-type mice (Supplementary Fig. ). Importantly, HE4 knockdown mice exhibited reduced PF. The extent and intensity of lung injury, and collagen accumulation, were significantly reduced in the lung tissues from HE4 knockdown mice (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). Consistent with these findings, the expression levels of fibrotic markers (collagen I, collagen III, α-SMA, and fibronectin) were significantly decreased in HE4 knockdown mice after BLM injury (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). Moreover, to rule out off-target effect, we administrated shRNA1 or shRNA2 lentivirus to BLM model mice. The results showed that shRNA1 or shRNA2 lentivirus administration significantly alleviated BLM-induced PF to varying degree. Moreover, the suppression of PF severity was correlated with knockdown efficiency (Supplementary Fig. ). Next, we analyzed the inflammatory response in HE4 knockdown mice at 7 days after BLM stimulation using shRNA3 (Supplementary Fig. ). H&E staining showed no major differences in alveolar wall thickness or inflammatory cell infiltration between BLM + HE4 scr shRNA-treated and BLM + HE4 shRNA-treated mice (Supplementary Fig. ). Consistent with these results, HE4 silencing did not affect the expression levels of the inflammation-related genes Il-1β , Il-6 , Mcp-1 , Ifn-γ , and Cxcl10 (Supplementary Fig. ). The results of recent studies have suggested that HE4 promotes cystic pulmonary fibrosis and renal fibrosis via MAPK and NF-κB signaling, respectively , . Thus, to investigate the impact of HE4 knockdown on downstream signaling pathways in PF, we evaluated the levels of critical signaling molecules in MAPK and NF-κB signaling pathways by western blotting using lung homogenates from mice stimulated with BLM for 21 days. The results showed that the p-ERK/ERK ratio was significantly decreased in the lungs of HE4 knockdown mice after BLM stimulation; However, HE4 knockdown did not cause significant changes in the ratio of p-JNK/JNK, p-p38/p38, or p-NF-κB p65/NF-κB p65 (Fig. ). Overall, these results indicate that HE4 silencing attenuates BLM-induced PF and ECM deposition without affecting the inflammatory response to lung injury. HE4 induces a profibrotic phenotype in epithelial cells and activates lung fibroblasts Many studies have shown that epithelial cell-secreted HE4 affects epithelial cell function through autocrine pathways , . To more fully elucidate the mechanism by which HE4 promotes PF, we used gain-of-function and loss-of function approaches in Beas-2B cells. We first detected the expression patterns of fibrosis genes in Beas-2B cells treated with various concentrations of recombinant human (rh) HE4 (0, 10 ng/ml, 20 ng/ml, 50 ng/ml) and/or TGFβ1. rhHE4 significantly increased the expression levels of fibrosis genes (Acta2, Col2a1, Fn1, vimentin, Ccn2, and Col1a2) in a concentration-dependent manner (from 10 to 50 ng/ml), as indicated by RT-qPCR (Supplementary Fig. ). Western blotting showed that Beas-2B cells treated with 50 ng/ml rhHE4 had significantly increased expression levels of fibronectin, collagen I, α-SMA, and p-ERK. However, compared with Beas-2B cells that had been treated with 4 ng/ml TGFβ1, cells treated with 50 ng/ml rhHE4 alone exhibited significantly lower induction of collagen I expression (Fig. ). In contrast, the expression levels of fibrosis markers (fibronectin, collagen I, and α-SMA) were decreased in siRNA-HE4-transfected Beas-2B cells (Supplementary Fig. ) compared with control (siRNA-NC-transfected) cells exposed to exogenous rhHE4 (Fig. ). These results indicated that rhHE4 induces the expression of fibrosis-related genes in epithelial cells in vitro by activating the ERK signaling. In IPF pathogenesis, aberrant crosstalk between the abnormal pulmonary epithelium and lung fibroblasts is central to disease progression , , . To determine whether secretory HE4 (sHE4) from epithelial cells affects fibroblast function, firstly, we overexpressed the HE4 gene in Beas-2B cells using an HE4 overexpression lentivirus. We found that introducing the HE4 expression vector (OE-HE4) led to increased HE4 protein secretion in the supernatant of Beas-2B cells (Supplementary Fig. ). Our previous results showed that BALF HE4 levels were increased in patients with IPF and mice with BLM induction (Supplementary Fig. and Fig. ). Altogether, these data indicated that epithelial cells derived HE4 is secreted to the extracellular medium. Next, we found that conditioned media from HE4-OE lentivirus-infected Beas-2B cells significantly increased the expression levels of fibrotic genes in MRC-5 cells (Supplementary Fig. ). Then, we treated MRC-5 cells with rhHE4 in vitro to further explore the role of sHE4 in lung fibroblast activation. CCK8 assays revealed that various concentration of rhHE4 (10 ng/ml, 20 ng/ml) had pro-proliferative effects on MRC-5 cells at multiple time points (Fig. ). Wound healing assays showed that 10 ng/ml or 20 ng/ml rhHE4 increased the migratory capacity of lung fibroblasts (Fig. ). Intriguingly, compared with control cells, rhHE4-treated MRC-5 cells displayed substantially increased RNA expression levels of Acta2, Fn1, Col1a2, and vimentin in a concentration-dependent manner, as indicated by RT-qPCR. However, the effect of rhHE4 on fibroblast activation was weaker than the effect of 4 ng/ml TGFβ1 (Supplementary Fig. ). Additionally, western blotting analysis showed that treatment with rhHE4 at 20 ng/ml significantly enhanced the expression levels of fibrotic markers, such as fibronectin, collagen I, and α-SMA, and activated ERK signaling (Fig. ). Therefore, we concluded that epithelial cell-secreted HE4 strongly promotes lung fibroblast activation in vitro by enhancing the level of phosphorylated ERK. HE4-ANXA2 binding enhances the profibrotic phenotype in epithelial cells and promotes lung fibroblast activation Next, we evaluated the regulatory effect of the HE4 and ANXA2 interaction on the profibrotic phenotype in epithelial cells. We transfected Beas-2B cells with siRNA-ANXA2, then confirmed the downregulations of ANXA2 RNA and protein expression levels in cells (Supplementary Fig. ). RT-qPCR and western blotting showed that interference with ANXA2 attenuated the exogenous rhHE4-induced expression of fibrosis-related genes in Beas-2B cells (Supplementary Fig. and Fig. ). Intriguingly, previous studies indicated that ANXA2 was also expressed on human lung fibroblasts . Therefore, we investigated whether the binding of HE4 to ANXA2 regulated lung fibroblast activation. The results showed that supplementation with extrinsically activated rhHE4 protein induced increases in fibrotic markers, which could be suppressed by ANXA2 silencing (Supplementary Fig. and Fig. ). Next, we performed in vitro and in vivo studies to determine whether HE4 regulated ANXA2 expression. We first examined the expression patterns of ANXA2 in Beas-2B and MRC-5 cells treated with various concentrations of rhHE4; we found that the upregulation of HE4 was not accompanied by significant changes in ANXA2 expression in either Beas-2B or MRC-5 cells (Fig. ). The results of animal experiments revealed that BLM stimulation led to increased ANXA2 expression in mouse lung tissue. However, ANXA2 expression was not significantly altered by HE4 knockdown (Fig. ). These data confirmed that increases or decreases in HE4 expression do not influence the expression of ANXA2. Intratracheal administration of HE4 shRNA lentivirus protects mice against BLM-induced PF Thus far, our data support a profibrotic role for HE4 in PF. Accordingly, we sought to translate the above discoveries into an anti-PF therapy. To determine the therapeutic effects of HE4 shRNA lentivirus administration in an in vivo model of PF, anesthetized C57BL/6 mice were intratracheally administered HE4 shRNA lentivirus at 7 days after BLM stimulation (Fig. ). The BLM-induced increase of HE4 protein expression was dramatically reduced in mouse lung tissue after administration of HE4 shRNA lentivirus (Supplementary Fig. ). This treatment significantly alleviated BLM-induced PF, as determined by histopathological analysis and fibrosis scores (Fig. ). Consistent with these findings, as shown in Fig. , lung tissues from mice administered HE4 shRNA lentivirus showed significant reductions in the expression levels of fibrotic markers (collagen I, collagen III, and fibronectin). Overall, these data suggest that targeting HE4 with HE4 shRNA-loaded lentivirus had therapeutic effects in a mouse model of established PF. Discussion IPF is a refractory disease, partially characterized by recurrent epithelial cell injury and the pathological accumulation of myofibroblasts that secrete ECM. More effective therapeutic options are needed; obstacle to new treatments is the limited understanding of molecular mechanisms underlying IPF pathogenesis. Our findings in the present study provide different insights concerning the regulation of pulmonary fibrogenesis and demonstrate a key role for lung epithelial cell-secreted HE4 in promoting PF. We provide evidence that HE4, a secreted glycoprotein, is associated with IPF severity while regulating phenotypic changes in lung epithelial cells and fibroblasts. Therefore, the targeted inactivation of HE4 could have potent anti-fibrotic effects in clinical settings. We obtained the following evidence to concerning the profibrotic role of lung epithelial cell-derived HE4 in pulmonary fibrogenesis. Effective knockdown of HE4, primarily in epithelial cells, significantly attenuated BLM-induced PF without affecting the inflammatory response in mice. In the gain-of-function model, systemic administration of rmHE4 exacerbated BLM-induced PF. HE4 belongs to the WFDC family of proteins, which is a relatively unexplored family of low-molecular-weight proteins. Thus far, most published studies of HE4 indicates that this small secretory protein constitutes a crucial fibrosis-associated molecule across various organs. In kidney fibrosis, HE4 was shown to have a pro-fibrogenic effect , . HE4 silencing inhibited ECM deposition and alleviated fibrosis in mice with unilateral ureteral obstruction . In dilated cardiomyopathy, HE4 induced cardiac interstitial fibrosis by activating cardiac fibroblasts . Additionally, published experimental evidence suggested the role of HE4 in fibrotic related respiratory diseases. HE4 reportedly destroys normal ECM and promote fibrosis in the setting of cystic PF ; it participates in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)-related airway remodeling . Intriguingly, reanalysis of HE4 gene expression in dataset GSE47460 revealed a significant increase among patients with IPF relative to patients with COPD, suggesting that HE4 levels are closely related to the extent of tissue remodeling and fibrosis. However, no significant difference in HE4 gene expression was detected between control participants and patients with COPD in dataset GSE47460 (Supplementary Fig. ), which contrasts with a previous study . This discrepancy may be due to the fact that these studies did not classify COPD patients, particularly those with fibrotic interstitial lung abnormality (ILA). ILA is a common radiologic finding in COPD, with patients with ILA having a higher risk of PF, which can manifest as subpleural interstitial fibrosis or fibroblast foci , . Therefore, future studies should assess the clinical relevance of HE4 levels in COPD patients with fibrotic ILA. Additionally, a recent report provided the first description of WFDC2 deficiency as a cause of chronic destructive airway disease , in contrast to ILDs – which show elevated WFDC2 expression patterns. Dougherty et al. also highlighted the etiology of chronic destructive airway disease caused by the deficiency of secreted WFDC2, indicating that protein replacement therapy may be a potential treatment option . This discrepancy may be explained that bronchiectasis in WFDC2 deficiency more closely mimics cystic fibrosis (all lobes) than IPF (lower lobes). Additionally, the pathological mechanisms underlying bronchiectasis and PF are different. The final common pathway in the pathological mechanisms underlying bronchiectasis results from a multifactorial combination of chronic or recurrent infection and an excessive inflammatory response, followed by abnormal lung tissues remodeling . However, IPF is generally not regarded as an inflammatory disease. Most importantly, Dougherty et al. demonstrated the phenotypic variation between mouse WFDC2 deficiency and human WFDC2 deficiency . Therefore, future studies should use humanized mouse model to further explore the function of WFDC2 in PF. The most notable finding in this report is that secretory HE4 contributes to PF pathogenesis by modulating phenotypic changes in lung epithelial cells and fibroblasts, two key target cells for PF. Recurrent and/or non-resolving injury to the lung epithelium is involved in initiating fibrosis. Although the initial cause of this injury in IPF remains unclear, it manifests as increased epithelial cell death and phenotypic changes in surviving epithelial cells . Next, we explored possible molecular mechanisms underlying the profibrotic effects of secretory HE4. We found that ANXA2 interacts with HE4; this protein binding interaction induces a profibrotic phenotype in epithelial cells and activates fibroblasts through aberrant epithelial-fibroblast crosstalk. Moreover, the presence of HE4-ANXA2 complex in the membranes of Beas-2B and MRC-5 cells indicated that HE4 secreted into the extracellular region could bind to the cell membranes of the epithelial cells themselves, as well as to those of adjacent fibroblasts. ANXA2 possesses both intracellular and extracellular roles. The interaction between ANXA2 and S100A4 can promote activation of matrix metalloproteinases, leading to ECM remodeling and neovascularization – . The results of previous studies suggested that ANXA2 is a specific target of BLM and plays a profibrotic role in PF , , . Moreover, in lung tissues, ANXA2 was located in epithelial cells and fibroblasts , indicating that secretory HE4 could bind to ANXA2 and mediate dual regulation of phenotypic changes in lung epithelial cells and fibroblasts. ANXA2 includes two forms: monomer and heterotetramer. The monomer is located to the cytoplasm, while the heterotetramer exits in the membrane . In certain cases, the ANXA2 monomer can migrate to the cell membrane to support different physiological functions, such as exocytosis, endocytosis, and membrane transport , . Previous studies have reported that HE4 and ANXA2, which co-localize in the cell membrane and cytoplasm, can interact in various malignant tumor cell types , . Secreted HE4 bounded to the membrane protein ANXA2 of the ovarian cancer cells themselves. This would allow ANXA2 to potentially facilitate HE4 translocation into the nucleus, where it can function as a transcription factor to promote the expression of downstream signaling molecules . Moreover, Wang et al. reported that HE4-ANXA2-MMP2 form a protein complex and promote the malignant of various cells migration . During this process, ANXA2 serves as “a bridge”. Our results showed the presence of HE4-ANXA2 complex on the cytoplasm and membrane of Beas-2B and MRC-5 cells. Preliminary data in present study indicated that HE4 is primarily secreted by epithelial cells, rarely by fibroblasts. Thus, the presence of HE4 and ANXA2 in the cytoplasm of MRC-5 cells suggested that ANXA2 may help HE4 translocate into the cells. Additionally, we found that increases or decreases in HE4 did not affect the expression of ANXA2. Therefore, we speculate that epithelial cell-derived HE4 is secreted into the extracellular medium, where it binds to ANXA2 on epithelial cell and fibroblasts membranes. ANXA2 may then help HE4 enter the cells, where it can activate downstream signaling molecules and induce phenotypic/behavioral changes. Methods Participants Microarray datasets of lung samples from healthy controls and patients with IPF ( GSE47460 ) were reanalyzed to determine HE4 RNA expression. Introduction Myeloid malignancies such as acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) are traditionally thought of as sporadic disorders. However, genetic predispositions to MDS/AML, also known as hereditary myeloid malignancy syndromes (HMMS), are becoming increasingly recognized. Several constitutional syndromes have long been known to predispose to myeloid malignancy, including Fanconi anemia, telomere biology disorders, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and Diamond-Blackfan anemia – . More recently, a growing number of HMMS without syndromic features caused by pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants in genes including RUNX1 , DDX41 , CEBPA , ETV6 , and ANKRD26 are relevant to MDS/AML care – . Despite these advancements, only 30% of families clustering MDS/AML have a P/LP variant identified, suggesting that additional causative genes remain to be discovered . HMMS are underrecognized due to limited provider awareness, insufficient recording of family history, and lack of HMMS-trained genetics providers in many areas. In addition, subtle clinical presentations, anticipation, variable expressivity, and phenotypic heterogeneity make establishing the diagnosis of HMMS challenging. Though the exact prevalence is unknown, HMMS are likely more common than previously recognized. Approximately 15% of patients with AML have a family history of hematologic malignancy . Of those evaluated in a hereditary clinic, 12–18% are ultimately diagnosed with a known HMMS , . Furthermore, in unselected MDS/AML populations, clinically actionable P/LP germline cancer susceptibility gene variants are identified in at least 7% of cases regardless of age , . Identification of HMMS is critical for optimizing care for patients and their families. Knowledge of HMMS may influence clinical management of the patient’s underlying MDS/AML, such as the decision to pursue hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT), choice of conditioning regimen, and donor selection, – or have implications for other organ and cancer surveillance , . Despite the importance of HMMS detection among patients with MDS/AML, there is no formal consensus as to which patients should undergo germline genetic evaluation, and expert-opinion recommendations for whom to test have evolved over time, making it difficult for providers to know who to refer. In 2021, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) added recommendations for germline genetic evaluation for patients meeting specific clinical and/or molecular criteria to the MDS and AML management guidelines , . However, data are lacking on the proportions of patients that will then need germline assessment as well as the practicality of implementing these guidelines in the care of patients with MDS/AML. Here, we report our single institution experience aiming to improve detection of HMMS by implementing NCCN MDS/AML germline genetic testing guidelines through a quality improvement (QI) committee. At the onset of our intervention, our institution had no standardized workflows for identifying those needing HMMS evaluation, for accessing HMMS evaluation at the appropriate level of urgency, or for reporting and reviewing somatic sequencing data for potential germline variants in patients with MDS/AML. Thus, we created a multidisciplinary QI committee to implement the systems-level changes required to facilitate germline genetic testing for patients with MDS/AML meeting guideline criteria. We report frequencies of patients meeting NCCN criteria, describe the proportions actually evaluated and tested and overall yield, and identify areas needing optimization to maximize detection of HMMS while minimizing burden on patient care and the healthcare system. Methods Patient Cohorts and Data Collection The post-intervention cohort consisted of patients with either newly diagnosed MDS/AML (including chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) and MDS/myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN) overlap) or those with new molecular data (e.g., relapsed AML with no prior multigene panel) between 9/1/2021 and 8/31/2022 who were prospectively reviewed by a hereditary hematology QI committee as described below. In order to assess the effectiveness of implementing this QI committee, data from patients newly diagnosed with MDS/AML between 1/1/2019 and 9/1/2021 with next-generation sequencing (NGS) data available were retrospectively reviewed (hereafter referred to as the pre-intervention cohort). For both cohorts, clinical, molecular, and family history data and germline genetic testing results (if applicable) were abstracted from the electronic medical record (EMR). This study was approved by the University of Wisconsin-Madison Institutional Review Board. Hereditary Hematology QI Committee Intervention On 7/1/2021, a hereditary hematology QI committee was formed to prospectively evaluate patients diagnosed with MDS/AML at our center for possible HMMS ( ). The committee first identified steps needed to implement NCCN guidelines within our institution including: 1) creating concise consensus criteria for HMMS evaluation encompassing both NCCN AML (version 1.2022) and MDS (3.2022) guidelines , ; 2) educating providers regarding key HMMS personal and family history details; 3) creating a system to capture all somatic NGS test results for centralized review; 4) adding a HMMS referral order to the EMR; 5) creating a concise referral recommendation template note for the EMR to be used to document reason for referral recommendation, degree of urgency, and how to refer the patient; and 6) developing a process for addressing urgent referrals. After finding solutions to the above steps, beginning on 9/1/2021, the committee met monthly to review each patient’s history and molecular data to determine if HMMS evaluation criteria were met ( ). These criteria consisted of clinical and molecular components. Clinical criteria were defined as 1) a personal or family history suggestive of an HMMS or other cancer predisposition syndrome ( ); 2) a family history of a hematologic cancer in a first-, second-, or third-degree relative; OR 3) MDS/AML diagnosed age ≤50 years. Molecular criteria were defined as the presence of a P/LP variant in ANKRD26 , CEBPA , DDX41 , ETV6 , GATA2 , RUNX1 , TERT , and/or TP53 at a variant allele frequency (VAF) of ≥30% detected on molecular genetic testing of MDS/AML cells using either a 57-gene (Myeloid Malignancies Mutation Panel; ARUP Laboratories, Salt Lake City, UT) or 42-gene (OncoHeme; Mayo Clinic Laboratories, Rochester, MN) panel. Variant interpretations were reassessed per American College of Medical Genetics and ClinGen Committee standards to identify those meeting P/LP status if confirmed in the germline , . For patients meeting criteria, a referral recommendation, documenting which criteria were met as well as the urgency of referral, was entered in the EMR ( ) and routed to the patient’s primary hematologist for review. If the patient was deceased or unable to pursue germline genetic evaluation for any reason at the time of QI committee review and suspicion for HMMS was strong (e.g. a known pathogenic recurrent germline DDX41 variant present on the patient’s somatic panel at a heterozygous VAF), our concerns, including risks, implications, and recommendations for family members, were communicated to the treating hematologist, who could then facilitate Genetics referral for at-risk relatives at his or her discretion. Urgent cases requiring expedited review were triaged within 24–48 hours by one or more committee members outside of regularly scheduled meetings when brought to the committee’s attention by the treating hematologist based on family history or by the molecular pathologist interpreting somatic sequencing results. If urgency was confirmed, a germline genetic evaluation was performed within one to two weeks. In all other cases, timing was determined on a case-by-case basis, occurring on average two to six weeks from initial referral. Genetic Evaluation Patients referred to Genetics underwent a comprehensive history and physical examination and family pedigree analysis by a certified genetic counselor (KSS) and cancer geneticist/hematologist/oncologist (JEC). All consenting patients with a clinical history or molecular data confirmed to meet the above criteria were offered germline genetic testing on cultured skin fibroblasts via a single or multigene panel personalized according to the individual patient scenario. Discussion In this study, we report our single institution experience using a hereditary hematology QI committee to implement current NCCN germline genetic testing criteria for patients with MDS/AML. In a cohort of 90 patients over a 12-month period, a surprisingly high proportion, 66%, met referral criteria for germline genetic evaluation. In addition, nearly half of referrals were considered urgent based on implications for treatment or transplant decision-making. Monthly review of patient history and molecular data as well as a formalized referral recommendation note in the EMR significantly increased guideline-concordant genetic referrals (14% versus 31%, p = 0.03). However, the majority of eligible patients were not referred at all, often due to critical illness, prolonged hospital stays, and early deaths. To our knowledge, this is the first study to prospectively test the clinical impact of implementing NCCN-based germline genetic testing referral criteria in an unselected MDS/AML patient population. This experience demonstrates that implementing current NCCN guidelines will significantly increase the proportion of patients referred and potentially diagnosed with HMMS. However, it also demonstrates the need for MDS/AML-specific models of genetic counseling and germline genetic testing, likely in the inpatient setting, to maximize benefit for patients and their families. With the yield of germline genetic testing for known HMMS in patients with MDS/AML being similar to germline genetic testing yields in other cancers for whom testing is recommended for all, – a universal screening strategy has been proposed, in which all patients diagnosed with MDS/AML undergo germline evaluation regardless of personal or family history , , . Our data, showing that the majority of patients with newly diagnosed MDS/AML will meet NCCN guidelines for germline genetic testing, and that nearly all who are evaluated and counseled will elect to proceed, support such a universal genetic testing approach. However, despite our QI committee increasing awareness of HMMS, providing formalized recommendations for Genetics referral, and having accessible, trained HMMS-focused genetic counselors and cancer geneticists, only ~30% of patients meeting criteria were ultimately referred. This was most often due to factors related to the high morbidity and mortality associated with an MDS/AML diagnosis. Specifically, nearly a third of eligible patients were deceased or enrolled in hospice at the time of our referral recommendation. Others were critically ill or were hospitalized for prolonged periods, precluding the typical outpatient genetic counseling and germline genetic evaluation workflow. Thus, our data highlight a critical need for urgent inpatient models of germline genetic evaluation for patients with MDS/AML, similar to those utilized for neonatal rapid whole exome sequencing, that will allow access close to the time of diagnosis when disease- and treatment-related morbidity is high, but which arguably is the optimal time for genetic evaluation to occur to assist in treatment planning. While implementation of a hereditary hematology QI committee was a significant time commitment for the members involved, we believe such a committee was essential for establishing a workflow for germline genetic evaluation for patients with MDS/AML. Having multiple myeloid malignancy providers as well as hematopathologists, molecular pathologists, cancer geneticists, and genetic counselors working together to ensure feasibility, clinical relevance, appropriate level of urgency, and buy-in from the broader hematology faculty at our institution was critical. As our data show, we identified many systems-level barriers to guideline-concordant genetic evaluation in this patient population, which our QI committee is now addressing. For example, we are training our hematology providers to ask HMMS questions during the initial history gathered for newly diagnosed patients, to recognize when patients need urgent referrals, and to perform skin biopsies for germline genetic testing purposes. When skin is collected at the time of diagnostic bone marrow biopsy, fibroblast culture and germline genetic testing results are expedited, which is especially important when outpatient Genetics evaluation will be delayed. Our genetic counseling team is also addressing barriers to inpatient genetic counseling services by enacting telephone/video visits for inpatients well enough to have these conversations. Introduction According to GLOBOCAN 2022, gastric cancer (GC) accounted for the fifth incidence with 968,000 novel cases and the fifth mortality with approximately 659,000 deaths among all malignant tumors ( ). China is a high-risk area for GC with a crude incidence rate of 254.1 per 100,000 and a crude mortality rate of 184.4 per 100,000 ( , ). Due to the atypical early symptoms of GC, most patients are already in the advanced stage when diagnosed ( ). There are several available options for advanced gastric cancer (AGC) treatment such as systemic chemotherapy, targeted therapies, and immunotherapy ( ). The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend a systemic chemotherapy regimen based on platinum combined with fluoropyrimidine drugs ( ). Even with conventional chemotherapy, the survival probability for AGC is still less than 1 year ( ). Although molecular targeted therapies, such as targeting human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR-2), and Claudin18.2, have achieved treatment improvement in recent years, not all patients’ tumor cells have specific targets ( ). Thus, chemotherapy and molecular targeted therapy have a limited impact on the overall prognosis of AGC. The advent of immunotherapy particularly immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has revolutionized the treatment landscape in recent years ( ). The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a number of anti-PD-1 antibodies for tumor treatment ( ). Based on various phase III clinical trials, such as ATTRACTION-2 phase III, CheckMate-649, ORIENT-16, RATIONALE-305, and KEYNOTE-859, anti-PD-1 antibodies have transitioned from a third-line option to a first-line treatment in AGC patients ( , – ). ICI treatment significantly gives an improved overall prognosis for AGC patients by enhancing the host’s endogenous immune response against the tumor ( ). The surveillance mechanisms of the host immune system play an important role in eliminating cancer, whereas tumors can express inhibitory signal molecules to suppress the immune function so as to achieve immune evasion via binding to their receptors on lymphocytes in the tumor microenvironment (TME) ( ). These inhibitory signal molecules and their corresponding receptors are commonly referred to as immune checkpoints including programmed cell death-1 (PD-1), programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1), and cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated 4 (CTLA-4) ( ). ICIs work by blocking immune checkpoints to restore the ability of the lymphocytes for tumor elimination ( ). However, the response to ICIs varies significantly among patients, leading to a hot research area for predicting individual responses ( – ). Previous studies have found that the appearance of immune-related adverse events (irAEs) may serve as a predictive indicator of good treatment outcomes ( – ). IrAEs occur from weeks to months after initiation of ICIs, affecting various organs and tissues such as the skin, gastrointestinal system, lungs, liver, adrenal gland, and thyroid with a single organ involved or multiple organs involved ( ). Some irAEs such as immune-related pneumonia, myocarditis, and enteritis can be fatal if they are not handled timely ( , ). Based on the number of affected organs, irAEs can be categorized as “single-organ irAE (uni-irAE)” (affecting only one organ) and “multi-organ irAEs (multi-irAEs)” (affecting more than one organ) ( ). Potential mechanisms for the development of irAEs include the common antigen between malignant cells and normal cells, the cross-immune response, off-target effects, B-cell activation and antibody-mediated damage, inflammatory cytokine-mediated damage, and the loss of peripheral tolerance in T cells caused by dysfunction of immune inhibitory cells ( – ). The occurrence of irAEs may signify the activation of the immune system, leading to continued attacks on tumor cells and causing sustained regression of the tumor. Previous studies have found that the emergence of irAEs was recognized as a key indicator of improved effectiveness of ICI treatment in various tumor types, including melanoma and small cell lung cancer (SCLC) ( , , , ). We and other researchers also revealed that the irAEs were associated with better OS and PFS in AGC patients ( , , ). However, the impact of irAEs on the treatment efficiency remains uncertain in AGC patients, so it does for the co-occurrence patterns of multi-irAEs ( ). Therefore, we evaluated the impact of the occurrence of irAEs including uni-irAE, multi-irAEs, and organ-specific irAE on both the therapeutic efficacy and prognosis of AGC patients with ICI treatment in the present study. The specific co-occurrence patterns of irAEs across multiple organs and their prognostic implications were also evaluated. All procedures were conducted in line with the Helsinki Declaration of 1964 and its later amendments and have been reviewed and sanctioned by the Ethics Committee of the Fourth Hospital of Hebei Medical University. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) the emergence of adverse events after initiation of immunotherapy; (2) pathological test results (if available); (3) diagnosed based on baseline disease status; (4) clinical improvement following irAE targeting therapies. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) the exclusion of other potential diagnoses with similar clinical manifestations; (2) determined by physicians that the adverse reaction is not caused by other medications (such as chemotherapy). IrAEs were classified based on the organ system affected (such as the skin, gastrointestinal tract, lungs, endocrine system, musculoskeletal system, kidneys, liver, nervous system, hematological system, and eyes). IrAEs were graded according to CTCAE and ranged from grade 1 to grade 5, which referred to mild, moderate, severe, life-threatening, or fatal events, depending on the severity of symptoms and the support of certain serum biomarkers. We defined irAEs affecting only a single organ as “uni-irAE” and those involving more than two organs as “multi-irAEs”. Consequently, the patients were categorized into three groups: those without any irAEs (non-irAE), those with uni-irAE, and those with multi-irAEs. Stable disease (SD) was defined as no change in the size of target lesions. The disease control rate (DCR) reflected the percentage of patients achieving a CR, PR, or SD. Discussion The occurrence of irAEs seemed to be a good predictor for ICI treatment in many cancer types including GC patients ( , , , ). The occurrence of irAEs is linked with better DCR and prolonged OS and PFS in AGC patients with nivolumab monotherapy; we also found that irAEs were associated with prolonged PFS in AGC patients, but few studies focus on the association of uni-irAE or multi-irAEs with the outcome of AGC patients ( , , ). In the present study, the multivariate analysis proved the association with both PFS and OS for multi-irAE AGC patients. Although the PFS extension of uni-irAE did not show statistical difference probably due to the small sample size, it displayed both the better DCR and the extension of OS in univariate analysis compared with the non-irAE group. Multiple centers with larger sample sizes are needed to confirm whether it is truly unrelated to PFS and OS. We also used the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression model suitable for small sample size analysis to verify these results. Notably, the results derived from these models aligned consistently with our initial findings referring to the association between multi-irAE and treatment outcomes (data not shown). These results are consistent with the results from the advanced renal cell carcinoma and SCLC, which suggest that the occurrence of irAEs indicates better survival, and multi-irAE patients exhibited an improved survival time than those of uni-irAE or non-irAE patients ( ). The precise mechanism underlying the enhanced efficacy of ICIs in patients with irAEs remains unclear, and few discussions regarding to the mechanism by which treatment efficacy of multi-irAEs is superior to uni-irAE. Functional experiments based on irAE-related experimental animals need to be performed to reveal the corresponding changes in the tumor microenvironment, including activated CD8, mature B cells, and even mature tertiary lymphoid structures, Treg cells, tumor associated macrophages, cytokines, etc. One hypothesis for irAE-mediated prognosis posits that ICIs reactivate exhausted T cells with cross-reactivity to both tumor and normal tissue antigens, resulting in enhanced antitumor immunity and irAEs ( ). However, some scholars also argue that the related immune response induced by ICIs may be non-specific, so it may attack both tumor and non-tumor cells indiscriminately ( ). Another possible explanation is that the inflammatory cytokine involved in the occurrence of irAEs could modify the treatment efficiency in cancer patients, and the patients carrying genetic variations near the interleukin-7 (IL-7) gene may have both a higher incidence of irAEs and improved survival. The abnormal expression of IL-7 might increase the stability of lymphocytes as well as block PD-1 to create a more favorable microenvironment corresponding to the ICI treatment ( , ). Another cytokine of interferon gamma (IFN-γ) also associated with both the occurrence of irAEs and better survival expectation ( – ). We had measured the blood cytokine levels of interleukin-2 (IL-2), interleukin-4 (IL-4), interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-10 (IL-10), IFN-γ, and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) between patients with and without irAEs, but no statistically significant differences were found (data not shown). We need to check other cytokines in the future. Thirdly, the gene mutations and expressing changes might be implicated in the occurrence of irAEs ( , ); we conducted an expression profiling analysis for blood microRNAs (miRNAs) including 16 miRNAs, which were proved to modify the AGC outcome with ICI treatment, but no candidate miRNA could be identified for their association with irAE occurrence (data not shown). Fourthly, the gut microbiota species and their metabolic pathway are involved in the occurrence of irAEs in GC patients; the gut microbiota species were also proved to enhance the treatment efficiency of ICI ( – ), so there is every chance that gut microbiota can mediate the irAE occurrence as well as modify the treatment efficiency.
